source_text: Πῶς δ᾿ οὐκ ἄντικρυς ψεῦδος τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαίου λεγόμενον, ὅτι μηδένα πείσας μέχρι ἔζη ὅ γε μηδὲ τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ μαθητὰς ἐκολάσθη καὶ τοιαῦτα ὑπέμεινε; πόθεν γὰρ ὁ φθόνος ὑπὸ τῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις ἀρχιερέων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων καὶ γραμματέων ἐκινήθη κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἢ ἐκ τοῦ πλήθη πειθόμενα ἀκολουθεῖν αὐτῷ καὶ εἰς τὰς ἐρημίας, κρατούμενα οὐ μόνον ὑπὸ τῆς τῶν λόγων αὐτοῦ ἀκολουθίας ἁρμόζοντα τοῖς ἀκούουσιν ἀεὶ λέγοντος, ἀλλὰ καὶ ταῖς δυνάμεσιν ἐκπλήττοντος τοὺς μὴ τῇ τοῦ λόγου αὐτοῦ ἀκολουθίᾳ πιστεύοντας; πῶς δ᾿ οὐκ ἄντικρυς ψεῦδος ὅτι οὐδὲ τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ ἔπεισε μαθητὰς, τοὺς παθόντας μὲν ἀνθρώπινόν τι ἀπὸ δειλίας τότε (οὐδέπω γὰρ ἦσαν πρὸς ἀνδρίαν ἠκονημένοι) οὐ μὴν τὰ κριθέντα αὐτοῖς ὡς περὶ Χριστοῦ ἀποθεμένους; ὁ μὲν γὰρ Πέτρος μετὰ τὸ ἀρνήσασθαι συναισθόμενος οἷ γέγονε κακῶν „ἐξελθὼν ἔξω ἔκλαυσε πικρῶς“· οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ πεπληγότες ὑπὸ τῆς ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ ἀθυμίας (ἔτι γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐθαύμαζον) ἐβεβαιώθησαν διὰ τῆς ἐπιφανείας αὐτοῦ πρὸς τὸ πιστεύειν ἔτι μᾶλλον καὶ βεβαιότερον παρὰ τὸ πρότερον ὅτι υἱὸς ἦν τοῦ θεοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: How is it not outright (ἄντικρυς) a lie (ψεῦδος), what is said by the Jew in Celsus, that having persuaded (πείθω) no one while he lived (ζάω), not even his own disciples (μαθητής), he was punished (κολάζω) and endured such things? For whence was the envy (φθόνος) stirred (κινέω) against him by the chief priests (ἀρχιερεύς) and elders (πρεσβύτερος) and scribes (γραμματεύς) among Jews, than from crowds (πλῆθος) persuaded to follow (ἀκολουθέω) him even into the deserts (ἐρημία), held (κρατέω) not only by the sequence/coherence (ἀκολουθία) of his words, always speaking things fitting (ἁρμόζω) to the hearers, but also by the powers (δυνάμεις) astonishing (ἐκπλήσσω) those not believing by the coherence of his word? How is it not outright a lie that he did not persuade even his own disciples, who suffered something human (ἀνθρώπινον) from cowardice (δειλία) then (for they were not yet whetted (ἀκονάω) to courage (ἀνδρεία)), yet did not put off (ἀποτίθημι) the things judged (κρίνω) by them as about Christ? For Peter after denying (ἀρνέομαι), perceiving (συναισθάνομαι) into what evils he had come, 'going out outside wept bitterly (πικρῶς)'; and the rest, struck (πλήσσω) by the despondency (ἀθυμία) over him (for still they admired (θαυμάζω) him), were confirmed (βεβαιόω) through his appearing (ἐπιφάνεια) to believe still more and more firmly than before that he was the Son of God.
pass_b_english: And how is it not an outright lie, what the Jew in Celsus says, that he “persuaded no one while he lived, not even his own disciples, and was punished and endured such things”? For where did the envy that the chief priests, elders and scribes of the Jews stirred up against him come from (Matthew 27:18; Mark 15:10), if not from the crowds who were persuaded to follow him even into desert places (Matthew 14:13)? They were held not only by the coherent order of his words, for he always spoke in a way that suited his hearers, but also by his mighty works, by which he astonished those who did not believe through the coherence of his word.

And how is it not an outright lie that he did not persuade even his own disciples? At that time they did suffer a human weakness out of cowardice, for their courage had not yet been sharpened; but they did not cast off the judgment they had formed about him as the Christ. For Peter, after his denial, realizing into what evil he had fallen, “went out and wept bitterly” (Matthew 26:75; Luke 22:62). And the rest, stricken with despondency over him (for they still admired him), were confirmed through his appearing, so that they believed still more, and more firmly than before, that he was the Son of God.

choices.why: ὁ φθόνος ὑπὸ τῶν ... ἀρχιερέων ... ἐκινήθη κατ᾿ αὐτοῦ: agency restored; 'envy stirred up among the chief priests' changed to 'envy that the chief priests, elders and scribes of the Jews stirred up against him'
πεπληγότες ... (ἔτι γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐθαύμαζον): concessive 'though' removed; the parenthesis explains their grief, it does not contrast with it
εἰς τὰς ἐρημίας: 'the deserts' changed to 'desert places'
οὐδέπω ... πρὸς ἀνδρίαν ἠκονημένοι: stiff 'sharpened to courage' changed to 'their courage had not yet been sharpened' (keeps Origen's image)
Checked: Matthew 27:18 and Mark 15:10 (envy), Matthew 14:13 (crowds follow into a desert place), Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62 (exact wording); the Jew's claim kept in quotation marks

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; English is from the Greek.

notes: Translated from the Greek of the staged Koetschau row only; Crombie (ANF) and Chadwick were not used.
Independent clause review: every clause checked; verdict pass.
Scripture citations sit inline beside the clause in Pass B.

translator_notes: Celsus’s words are given in quotation marks as reported (ὅτι with the Jew’s claim); the Greek ὅ γε is taken as ‘he who’. The envy of the leaders echoes Matthew 27:18 and Mark 15:10 (cited inline as allusions); the crowds following into deserted places echo Matthew 14:13 and parallels. ἀκολουθία has a play with ἀκολουθεῖν (‘follow’); rendered ‘coherent order’ / ‘coherence’. ‘Went out and wept bitterly’ (ἐξελθὼν ἔξω ἔκλαυσε πικρῶς) matches Matthew 26:75 and Luke 22:62 exactly. ἐπιφάνεια = his appearing after the resurrection; no single passage is quoted, so no citation added (cf. John 20:19–29). ἀθυμία rendered ‘despondency’; ἀνθρώπινόν τι παθόντες rendered ‘suffered a human weakness’.
